newsitem.title: USA: Detroit investment boom heals riot scars.
newsitem.headline: Detroit investment boom heals riot scars.

text.p: Thirty years after the worst U.S. riot of the 1960s left a swath of destruction and poverty in its wake, Detroit is experiencing a building and investment boom not seen in decades.

The construction bonanza, which includes twin sports stadiums, automotive components plants and the city's first new homes in three decades, is finally helping fix some of the deep scars left by the tragedy of July 23-27, 1967.
"I think things are looking up in Detroit," said Sidney Fine, a University of Michigan historian who wrote a 1989 book on the riot called "Violence in the Model City."

"They've got commitments for new investments, they've got an empowerment zone, the mayor has reached out to the suburbs and the suburbs are reciprocating," he said. "I wouldn't call it a booming metropolis, but things are looking up."

Since Mayor Dennis Archer took office in January 1994, replacing long-time Mayor Coleman Young, more than $5.74 billion worth of new private and public investment has been committed to the city, including more than $2 billion in new Chrysler Corp. plant expansions alone.
The city, helped by a $100 million federal empowerment zone designation, also is fielding bids to build up to three downtown casinos and working on plans to redevelop its substantial riverfront.

City officials, business leaders and residents hope the glitzy projects will help reverse a long-term decline that was accelerated by the riot, which prompted whites and businesses to flee to the suburbs.

"Those markers, once they are in place physically, will serve as a sign of great rennaissance," said Steven Chennault, a college English professor who grew up near the riot area. "I hope they don't fail in the way that the Renaissance Centre did," he said, referring to the tubular 1970s office complex that dominates Detroit's skyline.
On the city's near west side, vast areas burned out during the riot remain vacant and blighted as reminders of five of the most divisive days in Detroit's 296-year history.
Forty-four people were killed, 2,000 injured and 7,300 arrested in the disturbance, which was America's worst modern riot until 53 died in rioting in Los Angeles in 1992.

Many local experts attribute the riot to long-running oppression of blacks by the city's all-white police force. Tensions erupted in the early morning of Sunday, July 23, 1967, when police raided an illegal drinking club in a black neighbourhood.
As police hauled away 80 people, a crowd gathered and began taunting them, shouting that they would not have raided a white club. Many began throwing stones and looting stores.

Chennault, now 56, said he took photographs of some of the looters trying to break into a pawn shop, thwarting the attempt, and they almost turned on him. "The only thing that saved me was that I am black," he said.

By that Sunday evening, the situation was nearly out of control, with snipers keeping firefighters from extinguishing some of the 1,600 fires set in area buildings. The rioting did not subside until the following Thursday, two days after National Guard troops arrived.

Many white suburbanites still are reluctant to go into Detroit for fear of violence, but officials hope the new baseball and football stadiums, new restaurants and other projects will change attitudes and attract new residents to the city.

In June, the city cleared a major psychological hurdle with the peaceful celebration after the Detroit Red Wings hockey team won the Stanley Cup championship -- a far cry from the violence that had marred other sports titles in the 1980s and 1990s. A victory parade clogged downtown streets with more than 1 million fans, the city's biggest downtown gathering in decades.
But chronic problems with poverty, drugs, education and abandoned buildings remain in Detroit, which has shrunk to less than half its peak population of 2 million.
"They took a beating with the riots and lost an enormous amount of population and business," said Fine. "That was a lot to fix, but they're working on it."
